prompt.brief: Design a control plane for a distributed database that provisions clusters, manages topology and upgrades, scales capacity, detects failures, and safely reconciles desired state with live replicas.
successSignals: Keep cluster desired state, observed topology, node leases, operation plans, and database data-plane consensus separate.
Use a durable operation state machine and idempotent reconcilers for provisioning, failover, repair, resize, and upgrade.
Preserve quorum and fencing invariants while coordinating cloud APIs, disks, networking, certificates, and backups.
Explain tenant isolation, split brain, stuck operations, operator approval, rollback, and control-plane disaster recovery.

functional: Create clusters, add and remove replicas, change topology, rotate certificates, configure backups, and upgrade versions.
Expose operation progress, quorum health, replica lag, capacity, drift, failure reason, and safe next actions.
Support tenant-scoped roles, approvals for destructive operations, pause/resume, rollback, audit, and restore testing.
nonFunctional: Keep routine rolling operations within a bounded availability budget and never trade quorum safety for speed.
Manage thousands of clusters and tenants with cluster-scoped queues, leases, rate limits, and isolated reconcilers.
Make every provider action and topology transition idempotent, fenced, and recoverable after coordinator failure.
Continue serving safe status reads while queuing mutations when a provider, node group, or control-plane dependency fails.
scaleAssumptions: Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

dataFlow.title: Accept Cluster provisioning and configuration
dataFlow.description: The Control plane gateway authenticates the caller, validates the request, applies tenant policy and idempotency, then routes it to the owning service.

dataFlow.title: Commit the durable state
dataFlow.description: The control plane records versioned cluster intent and an idempotency key before asynchronous orchestration.

dataFlow.title: Publish the domain event
dataFlow.description: A durable outbox publishes committed Control plane events; consumers deduplicate by event ID and track offsets.

dataFlow.title: Build the read model
dataFlow.description: Partitioned workers consume Control plane events, update the serving projection, and expose lag or watermark metadata.

dataFlow.title: Serve and recover asynchronously
dataFlow.description: Serving reads use the Control plane projection; replay, repair, export, and slow work remain off the request path.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Control plane commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Control plane writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Control plane version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Control plane by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Control plane work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Control plane projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Control plane projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Control plane records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Control plane latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.

rubric.description: The answer defines cluster intent, reconciliation, quorum/failover, scale, durability, and failure contracts.
Entities and cluster/operation/node keys support provisioning, scaling, quorum, recovery, audit, and lifecycle changes.
Partitioning, cache behavior, queues, backpressure, and hot-key handling are explicit.
Idempotency, replay, recovery, degraded reads, and observability protect committed state.
The candidate can explain Control plane consistency, push/pull, managed services, and the scale boundary.
